LatentDiffusion/Variational.lean.title: The normalized variational problem
LatentDiffusion/Variational.lean.summary:
This section proves the variational characterization of the evidence. Let \(M\ge1\) be the number of data, let \(\mathcal A\) be an arbitrary set of parameters and let \(Z\) be a measurable space of latent variables. A posterior family consists of a real function \(\ell:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\), the log evidence, and, for each parameter \(a\in\mathcal A\) and each datum \(m\in\{1,\dots,M\}\), a probability measure \(\pi_a^m\) on \(Z\), the posterior of datum \(m\). For a collection \(q=(q^1,\dots,q^M)\) of probability measures on \(Z\), the free energy is

\[F(a,q)=-\ell(a)+\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\mathrm{KL}(q^m\|\pi_a^m),\]

where \(\mathrm{KL}\) denotes relative entropy. We prove that \(F(a,q)\ge-\ell(a)\), with equality exactly when \(q^m=\pi_a^m\) for every \(m\), and deduce the corrected form of the paper's Proposition 1: a pair \((a_\star,q_\star)\) minimizes \(F\) among all pairs with finite relative entropies if and only if \(a_\star\) maximizes \(\ell\) and \(q_\star^m=\pi_{a_\star}^m\) for every \(m\). No existence of a maximizer is asserted; existence and uniqueness are proved later from strong convexity of the marginal potential.

In the application \(\mathcal A\) is the space of parameters \(a=(\theta,\phi)\), \(\pi_a^m\) is the normalized tilted posterior \(Z_m(a)^{-1}e^{-U_m(a,z)}\,dz\) of datum \(m\), and \(\ell(a)=M^{-1}\sum_m\log Z_m(a)\) is the average tilted log evidence. The results hold for every parameter set and every measurable latent space, in particular for tilted models. The last step shows that a zero tilting penalty at a maximizer of the tilted evidence does not identify a maximizer of the original evidence, and gives a sufficient condition that does.

steps.title: Relative entropy, the free energy and its admissible domain
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(\mu\) and \( u\) be probability measures on \(Z\). If \(\mu\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \( u\) (written \(\mu\ll u\)), let \(d\mu/d u\) denote its Radon–Nikodym derivative. The relative entropy of \(\mu\) with respect to \( u\) is

\[\mathrm{KL}(\mu\| u)= egin{cases}\displaystyle\int_Z\log rac{d\mu}{d u}\,d\mu, & ext{if }\mu\ll u ext{ and }\log rac{d\mu}{d u}\in L^1(\mu),\ +\infty, & ext{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

It takes values in \([0,\infty]\). Gibbs' inequality states that the integral is nonnegative, and that \(\mathrm{KL}(\mu\| u)=0\) holds if and only if \(\mu= u\).

A posterior family is a pair \((\ell,\pi)\) as in the summary. A collection \(q=(q^m)_{m=1}^M\) of probability measures on \(Z\) is called admissible at \(a\in\mathcal A\) if

\[\mathrm{KL}(q^m\|\pi_a^m)<\infty\qquad ext{for every }m\in\{1,\dots,M\}.\]

To obtain a real-valued function on all pairs, write \(k(\mu\| u)=\mathrm{KL}(\mu\| u)\) when this number is finite and \(k(\mu\| u)=0\) otherwise. The free energy is

\[F(a,q)=-\ell(a)+ rac1M\sum_{m=1}^Mk(q^m\|\pi_a^m),\qquad(1)\]

with \(1/M\) read as \(0\) when \(M=0\). On admissible pairs \(k\) coincides with \(\mathrm{KL}\), so (1) is the free energy of the summary. Every minimization statement below is restricted to admissible pairs; the convention for infinite values therefore never enters a conclusion about minimizers. Finally, \((a,q)\) is a global minimizer if \(q\) is admissible at \(a\) and \(F(a,q)\le F(b,r)\) for every \(b\in\mathcal A\) and every collection \(r\) admissible at \(b\).

steps.title: The posterior attains the variational lower bound
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((\ell,\pi)\) be a posterior family with \(M\in\mathbb N\) data and let \(a\in\mathcal A\). Then

  1. the posterior collection \(\pi_a=(\pi_a^m)_m\) is admissible at \(a\);
  2. \(F(a,\pi_a)=-\ell(a)\);
  3. \(-\ell(a)\le F(a,q)\) for every collection \(q\) of probability measures, admissible or not.

Proof. (1) Let \( u\) be a probability measure. Then \( u\ll u\) and \(d u/d u=1\) holds \( u\)-almost everywhere, so \(\log(d u/d u)=0\) almost everywhere. This function is integrable and its integral is \(0\). Hence \(\mathrm{KL}( u\| u)=0<\infty\). Applying this with \( u=\pi_a^m\) for each \(m\) proves admissibility.

(2) By (1) every summand of (1) of the previous step vanishes, so \(F(a,\pi_a)=-\ell(a)+M^{-1}\cdot0=-\ell(a)\).

(3) Each number \(k(q^m\|\pi_a^m)\) is nonnegative: it is either a finite value of \(\mathrm{KL}\), which lies in \([0,\infty)\), or \(0\). The factor \(1/M\) is nonnegative, also when it is read as \(0\). Hence the second term of \(F(a,q)\) is nonnegative and \(F(a,q)\ge-\ell(a)\). \(\square\)

Rearranged, (3) is the evidence lower bound \(\ell(a)\ge-F(a,q)\), and (2) shows that it is attained at the posterior.

steps.title: Equality in the variational bound
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(M\ge1\), let \(a\in\mathcal A\) and let \(q\) be admissible at \(a\). Then

\[F(a,q)=-\ell(a)\iff q^m=\pi_a^m\text{ for every }m\in\{1,\dots,M\}.\]

Proof. (\(\Leftarrow\)) If \(q=\pi_a\), the previous step gives \(F(a,q)=-\ell(a)\).

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Write \(k_m=\mathrm{KL}(q^m\|\pi_a^m)\). By admissibility each \(k_m\) is a finite number in \([0,\infty)\), and \(F(a,q)=-\ell(a)+M^{-1}\sum_mk_m\). If \(F(a,q)=-\ell(a)\), then \(M^{-1}\sum_mk_m=0\). Because \(M\ge1\), the factor \(M^{-1}\) is nonzero, so \(\sum_mk_m=0\). A finite sum of nonnegative real numbers vanishes only if every summand vanishes; hence \(k_m=0\) for every \(m\). By the equality case of Gibbs' inequality, \(\mathrm{KL}(q^m\|\pi_a^m)=0\) implies \(q^m=\pi_a^m\). \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(M\ge1\) is used only to cancel the factor \(1/M\). Admissibility is needed because an infinite relative entropy contributes \(0\) to the real-valued formula (1); without it, the vanishing of the real sum would not imply the vanishing of the relative entropies.

steps.title: Characterization of the global minimizers
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(M\ge1\), \(a\in\mathcal A\), and let \(q\) be a collection of \(M\) probability measures on \(Z\). Then \((a,q)\) is a global minimizer of \(F\) if and only if

\[\ell(b)\le\ell(a)\ \text{ for every }b\in\mathcal A\qquad\text{and}\qquad q^m=\pi_a^m\ \text{ for every }m.\]

Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) Let \((a,q)\) be a global minimizer; in particular \(q\) is admissible at \(a\). The posterior collection \(\pi_a\) is admissible at \(a\), so minimality and the posterior identity of the second step give

\[F(a,q)\le F(a,\pi_a)=-\ell(a).\]

The lower bound of the second step gives \(F(a,q)\ge-\ell(a)\); hence \(F(a,q)=-\ell(a)\), and the previous step yields \(q=\pi_a\). Now let \(b\in\mathcal A\). Since \(\pi_b\) is admissible at \(b\), minimality gives

\[-\ell(a)=F(a,q)\le F(b,\pi_b)=-\ell(b),\]

that is, \(\ell(b)\le\ell(a)\).

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Suppose \(a\) maximizes \(\ell\) and \(q=\pi_a\). Then \(q\) is admissible at \(a\). For every \(b\) and every \(r\) admissible at \(b\), the posterior identity, the maximality of \(a\) and the lower bound at \(b\) give

\[F(a,\pi_a)=-\ell(a)\le-\ell(b)\le F(b,r).\]

Thus \((a,\pi_a)\) is a global minimizer. \(\square\)

The statement asserts neither that \(\ell\) has a maximizer nor that a maximizer is unique; both questions are settled later for strongly convex potentials. The normalized posterior collection is the unique optimal variational collection at each maximizer.

steps.title: Evidence maximizers are the parameter components of minimizers
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(M\ge1\) and \(a\in\mathcal A\). Then \(a\) maximizes \(\ell\) if and only if there is a collection \(q\) such that \((a,q)\) is a global minimizer of \(F\).

Proof. If \(a\) maximizes \(\ell\), the previous step applied with \(q=\pi_a\) shows that \((a,\pi_a)\) is a global minimizer. Conversely, if \((a,q)\) is a global minimizer for some \(q\), the forward direction of the previous step shows that \(a\) maximizes \(\ell\). \(\square\)

steps.title: A zero tilting gap at a tilted maximizer is not sufficient
steps.body:
The paper optimizes a tilted evidence \(\tilde\ell\le\ell\). This step compares maximizers of \(\tilde\ell\) with those of the original evidence \(\ell\).

Claim 1 (sufficient condition). Let \(\ell,\tilde\ell:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(\tilde\ell(x)\le\ell(x)\) for all \(x\). Let \(b\) maximize \(\ell\) with \(\tilde\ell(b)=\ell(b)\), and let \(a\) maximize \(\tilde\ell\). Then \(\ell(a)=\ell(b)\); in particular \(a\) maximizes \(\ell\).

Proof. Maximality of \(a\) for \(\tilde\ell\), the zero gap at \(b\), the comparison \(\tilde\ell\le\ell\) at \(a\), and maximality of \(b\) for \(\ell\) give

\[\ell(b)=\tilde\ell(b)\le\tilde\ell(a)\le\ell(a)\le\ell(b).\]

All inequalities are therefore equalities, and \(\ell(a)=\ell(b)\). \(\square\)

Claim 2 (counterexample). On the two-point set \(\mathcal A=\{0,1\}\) let \(\ell(0)=0\), \(\ell(1)=1\) and let the gap \(g=\ell-\tilde\ell\) be \(g(0)=0\), \(g(1)=2\). Then \(g\ge0\), \(g(0)=0\), the point \(0\) maximizes \(\tilde\ell=\ell-g\), and \(\ell(0)<\ell(1)\).

Proof. The tilted values are \(\tilde\ell(0)=0\) and \(\tilde\ell(1)=1-2=-1\), so \(0\) maximizes \(\tilde\ell\). The remaining assertions are the numerical facts \(0\le0\), \(0\le2\) and \(0<1\). \(\square\)

Thus a zero penalty at the tilted maximizer itself does not imply that it maximizes the original evidence. Claim 1 shows what does: a maximizer of the original evidence at which the tilting gap vanishes.

LatentDiffusion/Marginal.lean.title: The marginal evidence and its unique maximizer
LatentDiffusion/Marginal.lean.summary:
For each datum \(m\in\{1,\dots,M\}\) let \(U_m:\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_z}\to\mathbb R\) be the joint potential, the negative logarithm of the tilted joint density of the parameter \(a\) and the latent variable \(z\). The pair space carries the Euclidean norm \(\|(a,z)\|^2=\|a\|^2+\|z\|^2\). Assumption A3 states that each \(U_m\) is differentiable and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex with one constant \(\lambda>0\):

\[U_m(sx+(1-s)y)\le sU_m(x)+(1-s)U_m(y)-\frac\lambda2s(1-s)\|x-y\|^2\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_z},\ s\in[0,1]).\]

The normalizer and the marginal potential of datum \(m\) are

\[Z_m(a)=\int_{\mathbb R^{d_z}}e^{-U_m(a,z)}\,dz,\qquad V_m(a)=-\log Z_m(a),\qquad V(a)=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^MV_m(a)=-\ell(a),\]

so \(V\) is minus the average log evidence \(\ell\). This section proves that \(V\) is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, tends to \(+\infty\) at infinity and has exactly one minimizer \(a_\star\); that for every posterior family with log evidence \(-V\) the free energy has exactly one global minimizer \((a_\star,\pi_{a_\star})\); and that \(V\) grows quadratically away from \(a_\star\). The last step quantifies the effect of the tilting on the optimizer. The unique minimizer is the target of all convergence results of this report.

steps.title: Strong convexity of the average marginal potential
steps.body:
Two facts about a single joint potential are used; they are proved in the companion report on interacting particle Langevin algorithms. Let \(U\) be differentiable and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_z}\) with \(\lambda>0\), and put \(Z_U(a)=\int e^{-U(a,z)}dz\).

  • (Integrability.) For each \(a\), the function \(z\mapsto e^{-U(a,z)}\) is Lebesgue integrable and \(Z_U(a)>0\). Indeed, strong convexity gives \(U(x)\ge U(0)-\|\nabla U(0)\|^2/\lambda+\frac\lambda4\|x\|^2\), so \(e^{-U(a,z)}\le Ce^{-\lambda\|z\|^2/4}\), and an integral of a positive continuous function is positive.
  • (Prékopa–Leindler.) The marginal potential \(a\mapsto-\log Z_U(a)\) is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, with the same constant \(\lambda\).

Claim. Let \(M\ge1\), \(\lambda>0\), and let every \(U_m\) be differentiable and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex. Then \(V=M^{-1}\sum_mV_m\) is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex: for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) and all \(\alpha,\beta\ge0\) with \(\alpha+\beta=1\),

\[V(\alpha x+\beta y)\le\alpha V(x)+\beta V(y)-\alpha\beta\,\frac\lambda2\|x-y\|^2.\]

Proof. By the Prékopa–Leindler fact applied to \(U=U_m\), for each \(m\),

\[V_m(\alpha x+\beta y)\le\alpha V_m(x)+\beta V_m(y)-\alpha\beta\,\frac\lambda2\|x-y\|^2.\]

Summing over the \(M\) data, the last term contributes \(M\alpha\beta\frac\lambda2\|x-y\|^2\). Multiplying by \(1/M\ge0\) preserves the inequality and gives

\[V(\alpha x+\beta y)\le\alpha V(x)+\beta V(y)-\frac MM\,\alpha\beta\,\frac\lambda2\|x-y\|^2.\]

Since \(M\ge1\), \(M/M=1\). \(\square\)

The constant is not divided by \(M\) because the potentials are averaged. Averaging is the normalization used throughout this report.

steps.title: Coercivity of the marginal potentials
steps.body:
A third fact from the companion report is used: under the hypotheses of the previous step, \(Z_U(a)\to0\) as \(\|a\|\to\infty\).

Claim. (1) If \(U\) is differentiable and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex with \(\lambda>0\), then \(-\log Z_U(a)\to+\infty\) as \(\|a\|\to\infty\). (2) If in addition \(M\ge1\) and every \(U_m\) satisfies these hypotheses, then \(V(a)\to+\infty\) as \(\|a\|\to\infty\).

Proof. (1) By the cited fact and positivity of \(Z_U\), \(Z_U(a)\) tends to \(0\) through positive values. Since \(\log t\to-\infty\) as \(t\downarrow0\), the composition \(\log Z_U(a)\to-\infty\), and its negative tends to \(+\infty\).

(2) Let \(B\in\mathbb R\). By (1), for each \(m\) there is \(R_m\) with \(V_m(a)\ge B\) whenever \(\|a\|\ge R_m\). Put \(R=\max_mR_m\), a maximum over finitely many numbers. For \(\|a\|\ge R\), all \(M\) inequalities hold, and averaging them gives

\[V(a)=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^MV_m(a)\ge\frac1M\cdot MB=B.\]

Since \(B\) was arbitrary, \(V(a)\to+\infty\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Existence and uniqueness of the minimizer
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(M\ge1\), \(\lambda>0\), and let every \(U_m\) be differentiable and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex. Then there is exactly one \(a_\star\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) with \(V(a_\star)\le V(a)\) for all \(a\). Equivalently, the average log evidence \(\ell=-V\) has exactly one maximizer.

Proof. Continuity. Each \(V_m\) is continuous (companion report: the normalizer is continuous and positive, and \(\log\) is continuous on \((0,\infty)\)); hence \(V\), a constant multiple of a finite sum, is continuous.

Existence. Fix \(a_0\). By the previous step there is \(R\) with \(V(a)>V(a_0)\) for \(\|a\|\ge R\). The closed ball \(\bar B_R=\{\|a\|\le R\}\) is compact (Heine–Borel) and nonempty, since \(a_0\in\bar B_R\). A continuous function on a nonempty compact set attains its minimum, say at \(a_\star\in\bar B_R\). Then \(V(a_\star)\le V(a)\) for \(a\in\bar B_R\), and for \(\|a\|\ge R\) we have \(V(a)>V(a_0)\ge V(a_\star)\). Thus \(a_\star\) is a global minimizer.

Uniqueness. Let \(a\) and \(b\) both be global minimizers, so \(V(a)=V(b)=\min V\). Strong convexity with \(\alpha=\beta=\frac12\) gives

\[V\Bigl(\frac{a+b}2\Bigr)\le\frac{V(a)+V(b)}2-\frac\lambda8\|a-b\|^2=\min V-\frac\lambda8\|a-b\|^2.\]

If \(a\ne b\), the right side is strictly smaller than \(\min V\) because \(\lambda>0\), which is impossible. Hence \(a=b\). \(\square\)

steps.title: The unique variational optimizer
steps.body:
Recall from the variational section: for a posterior family \((\ell,\pi)\) with \(M\ge1\) data, \((a,q)\) is a global minimizer of \(F(a,q)=-\ell(a)+M^{-1}\sum_m\mathrm{KL}(q^m\|\pi_a^m)\) over admissible pairs if and only if \(a\) maximizes \(\ell\) and \(q^m=\pi_a^m\) for all \(m\).

Claim. Let \(M\ge1\), \(\lambda>0\), and let every \(U_m\) be differentiable and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex. Let \(Z\) be any measurable space and \((\ell,\pi)\) any posterior family on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) and \(Z\) whose log evidence is \(\ell(a)=-V(a)\) for every \(a\). Then there is exactly one pair \((a,q)\) that is a global minimizer of \(F\), namely \((a_\star,\pi_{a_\star})\) with \(a_\star\) the minimizer of \(V\).

Proof. Existence. Let \(a_\star\) be the minimizer of the previous step. For every \(b\), \(\ell(b)=-V(b)\le-V(a_\star)=\ell(a_\star)\), so \(a_\star\) maximizes \(\ell\). By the characterization, \((a_\star,\pi_{a_\star})\) is a global minimizer.

steps.title: Quadratic growth at a minimizer
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real normed vector space, \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), and \(F:H\to\mathbb R\) \(\lambda\)-strongly convex on \(H\). If \(z\) minimizes \(F\), then for every \(x\in H\),

\[\frac\lambda2\|x-z\|^2\le F(x)-F(z).\]

No differentiability of \(F\) is assumed.

Proof. Fix \(x\) and let \(0<s<1\). Strong convexity with the weights \(1-s\) and \(s\) at the points \(z\) and \(x\) gives

\[F((1-s)z+sx)\le(1-s)F(z)+sF(x)-(1-s)s\,\frac\lambda2\|z-x\|^2.\]

Minimality of \(z\) gives \(F(z)\le F((1-s)z+sx)\). Combining the two inequalities and subtracting \((1-s)F(z)\),

\[s\cdot\frac\lambda2(1-s)\|x-z\|^2\le s\,\bigl(F(x)-F(z)\bigr).\]

Dividing by \(s>0\) gives \(\frac\lambda2(1-s)\|x-z\|^2\le F(x)-F(z)\) for every \(s\in(0,1)\). The left side is a continuous function of \(s\) with limit \(\frac\lambda2\|x-z\|^2\) as \(s\downarrow0\), and a limit of numbers bounded above by \(F(x)-F(z)\) is bounded by the same number. \(\square\)

steps.title: Simultaneous control of parameter and posterior errors
steps.body:
Claim. Assume the hypotheses of the unique-optimizer step: \(M\ge1\), \(\lambda>0\), every \(U_m\) differentiable and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, and \((\ell,\pi)\) a posterior family with \(\ell=-V\). Let \(a_\star\) minimize \(V\). Then for every parameter \(a\) and every collection \(q\) of probability measures,

\[\frac\lambda2\|a-a_\star\|^2+\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^Mk(q^m\|\pi_a^m)\le F(a,q)-F(a_\star,\pi_{a_\star}),\]

where \(k\) is the relative entropy with infinite values replaced by \(0\), as in the definition of \(F\). For admissible \(q\) the second term is the average relative entropy to the posteriors.

\[F(a,q)-F(a_\star,\pi_{a_\star})=V(a)-V(a_\star)+\frac1M\sum_mk(q^m\|\pi_a^m).\]

By strong convexity of \(V\) and the quadratic growth step, \(V(a)-V(a_\star)\ge\frac\lambda2\|a-a_\star\|^2\). Substituting this bound proves the claim. \(\square\)

steps.title: Robustness of the optimizer to the tilting bias
steps.body:
Let \(\ell\) be the original evidence and \(\tilde\ell\) the tilted evidence, both real functions on a set \(\mathcal A\).

Claim 1. Let \(\delta,\varepsilon\in\mathbb R\). Assume a one-sided uniform gap \(0\le\ell(x)-\tilde\ell(x)\le\delta\) for all \(x\), and that \(\hat a\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-maximizer of \(\tilde\ell\): \(\tilde\ell(x)\le\tilde\ell(\hat a)+\varepsilon\) for all \(x\). Then \(\ell(a)-\ell(\hat a)\le\delta+\varepsilon\) for every \(a\in\mathcal A\).

Proof. The gap bound at \(a\), the \(\varepsilon\)-maximality, and the lower gap bound at \(\hat a\) give

\[\ell(a)\le\tilde\ell(a)+\delta\le\tilde\ell(\hat a)+\varepsilon+\delta\le\ell(\hat a)+\varepsilon+\delta.\qquad\square\]

Claim 2. Let \(H\) be a real normed vector space, \(\lambda>0\), \(\delta,\varepsilon\ge0\), and suppose \(-\ell\) is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex on \(H\). Assume the gap and \(\varepsilon\)-maximality conditions of Claim 1 and let \(a_\star\) maximize \(\ell\). Then

\[\|\hat a-a_\star\|\le\sqrt{\frac{2(\delta+\varepsilon)}\lambda}.\]

Proof. Quadratic growth of \(-\ell\) at its minimizer \(a_\star\) gives \(\frac\lambda2\|\hat a-a_\star\|^2\le\ell(a_\star)-\ell(\hat a)\), and Claim 1 bounds the right side by \(\delta+\varepsilon\). Dividing by \(\lambda/2>0\) gives \(\|\hat a-a_\star\|^2\le2(\delta+\varepsilon)/\lambda\). Both sides are nonnegative, so the inequality between their square roots follows from monotonicity of the square root. \(\square\)

This section constructs the tilted latent model from the joint potentials \(U_1,\dots,U_M\) of assumption A3 and identifies its optimizer. \[\widetilde F(a,q)=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\int_{\mathbb R^{d_z}}\tilde q^m(z)\log\frac{\tilde q^m(z)}{\rho_a^m(z)}\,dz\]

on the domain of collections \(q\) with finite relative entropies and finite second moments; here \(\tilde q^m\) is the Lebesgue density of \(q^m\).

\[U_a(\alpha x+\beta y)\le\alpha U_a(x)+\beta U_a(y)-\alpha\beta\,\frac\lambda2\|x-y\|^2,\]

steps.title: The density model and its evidence
steps.body:

A density model with \(M\) data consists of functions \(\rho_a^m:Z\to\mathbb R\), indexed by parameters \(a\) and data \(m\), such that each \(\rho_a^m\) is measurable, strictly positive and \(\nu\)-integrable with \(Z_m(a)=\int\rho_a^m\,d\nu>0\). Its posteriors are \(\pi_a^m(dz)=Z_m(a)^{-1}\rho_a^m(z)\,\nu(dz)\); these are probability measures, because the density \(\rho_a^m/Z_m(a)\) is nonnegative and has integral \(Z_m(a)/Z_m(a)=1\). Claim. Let \(\lambda>0\) and let every \(U_m\) be differentiable and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex. Then \(\rho_a^m(z)=e^{-U_m(a,z)}\), with \(\nu\) Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R^{d_z}\), is a density model, and its log evidence satisfies

\[\ell(a)=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\log Z_m(a)=-V(a)\qquad\text{for every }a.\]

By the previous step the slice \(z\mapsto U_m(a,z)\) is differentiable, hence continuous; composing with the continuous functions \(t\mapsto-t\) and \(\exp\) gives a continuous, hence Borel measurable, function. steps.title: The posteriors have finite second moments

Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step, for every \(a\) and every \(m\),

\[\int_{\mathbb R^{d_z}}\|z\|^2\,\pi_a^m(dz)<\infty.\]

Hence \(\int\|z\|^2\,d\pi_a^m=\int\|z\|^2\,d\gamma_W<\infty\). \(\square\)

LatentDiffusion/RegularFlowCalculus.lean.summary:
This section proves the de Bruijn identity for the joint parameter–density flow of the paper,.

The extra assumptions are Extra A2 and Extra A3.

The latent space \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner product space with Lebesgue measure, and the parameter space \(A\) is a complete real inner product space. For probability densities \(q^1,\dots,q^M\) on \(E\), potentials \(U_m:A\times E\to\mathbb R\) and a parameter \(a\), define the normalized density energy, the averaged parameter force and the Fisher information

\[\mathcal E(a,q)=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\int_Eq^m(\log q^m+U_m(a,\cdot))\,dz,\qquad G(a,q)=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\int_Eq^m\,\nabla_aU_m(a,\cdot)\,dz,\] \[I(a,q)=\|G(a,q)\|^2+\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\int_Eq^m\,\bigl\|\nabla_z\bigl(\log q^m+U_m(a,\cdot)\bigr)\bigr\|^2\,dz.\]

When \(q^m\) is the density of a probability measure \(Q^m\) and the integrals are finite, \(\int q^m(\log q^m+U_m(a,\cdot))\,dz=\mathrm{KL}(Q^m\|\pi_a^m)-\log Z_m(a)\), so \(\mathcal E(a,q)\) is the free energy \(F(a,Q)\) of the variational section, written as the paper's literal integral. The flow is the parameter equation \(\dot a_t=-G(a_t,q_t)\) together with the Fokker–Planck equations \(\partial_tq_t^m=\nabla\cdot\bigl(q_t^m\nabla(\log q_t^m+U_m(a_t,\cdot))\bigr)\). The main result is

\[\frac{d}{dt}\,\mathcal E(a_t,q_t)=-I(a_t,q_t).\]

Its proof has three ingredients: differentiation under the integral sign, justified by local domination; Lebesgue integration by parts on the unbounded space \(E\), justified by integrability of three explicit products; and the chain rule in the parameter. Along the way we obtain the gradient of \(\mathcal E\) for the normalized product metric \(d^2=\|a-b\|^2+M^{-1}\sum_mW_2(q^m,r^m)^2\): its parameter component is \(G\) and its \(m\)-th density component is \(\nabla(\log q^m+U_m)\), with no factor \(1/M\). The identity is used in the convergence theorem for the classical flow; the integration-by-parts identities are also used for the entropy tangent inequality of the transport section.

\[\dot q\,\bigl(\log q(t)+U(t)+1\bigr)+q(t)\,\dot U.\]

\[\dot q\,\bigl(\log q(t)+U(t)\bigr)+q(t)\Bigl(\frac{\dot q}{q(t)}+\dot U\Bigr)=\dot q\,\bigl(\log q(t)+U(t)\bigr)+\dot q+q(t)\dot U,\]

which is the stated expression. \(\square\)

Setting. Let \(\nu\) be a measure on a measurable space \(X\), and let \(q,\dot q,U,\dot U:\mathbb R\times X\to\mathbb R\), written \(q_u(x)\) and so on. The density energy at time \(u\) is

\[\mathcal E(u)=\int_Xq_u(x)\bigl(\log q_u(x)+U_u(x)\bigr)\,\nu(dx),\]

and the candidate derivative integrand is \(\varphi_u(x)=\dot q_u(x)\bigl(\log q_u(x)+U_u(x)+1\bigr)+q_u(x)\dot U_u(x)\).

Local domination at \(t\) consists of a neighbourhood \(N\) of \(t\) and a function \(g:X\to\mathbb R\) such that

  1. for all \(u\) near \(t\), the integrand \(x\mapsto q_u(x)(\log q_u(x)+U_u(x))\) is measurable, and it is \(\nu\)-integrable for \(u=t\);
  2. \(\varphi_t\) is measurable;
  3. for \(\nu\)-almost every \(x\), \(|\varphi_u(x)|\le g(x)\) for all \(u\in N\), and \(g\) is \(\nu\)-integrable;
  4. for \(\nu\)-almost every \(x\) and all \(u\in N\), \(q_u(x)>0\) and \(u\mapsto q_u(x)\) has derivative \(\dot q_u(x)\) at \(u\).

The local differentiation assumptions additionally require: (5) for \(\nu\)-almost every \(x\) and all \(u\in N\), \(u\mapsto U_u(x)\) has derivative \(\dot U_u(x)\) at \(u\). Measurability is understood up to \(\nu\)-null sets.

Claim. Under the local differentiation assumptions at \(t\), \(\varphi_t\) is \(\nu\)-integrable and \(\mathcal E\) is differentiable at \(t\) with

\[\mathcal E'(t)=\int_X\varphi_t\,d\nu.\]

Proof. We use the theorem on differentiation under the integral sign: let \(F(u,x)\) be measurable in \(x\) for \(u\) near \(t\), with \(F(t,\cdot)\) integrable; suppose that for almost every \(x\) the function \(u\mapsto F(u,x)\) has derivative \(F'(u,x)\) for every \(u\) in a neighbourhood \(N\) of \(t\), with \(|F'(u,x)|\le g(x)\) for \(u\in N\) and \(g\) integrable, and that \(F'(t,\cdot)\) is measurable. Then \(F'(t,\cdot)\) is integrable and \(u\mapsto\int F(u,x)\,dx\) has derivative \(\int F'(t,x)\,dx\) at \(t\). (The proof: by the mean value inequality, \(|F(u,x)-F(t,x)|\le g(x)|u-t|\) for \(u\) in a ball inside \(N\), so the difference quotients are dominated by \(g\); dominated convergence passes to the limit.)

Apply it with \(F(u,x)=q_u(x)(\log q_u(x)+U_u(x))\) and \(F'=\varphi\). Hypotheses (1)–(3) are its measurability, integrability and domination conditions. For almost every \(x\) and every \(u\in N\), hypotheses (4) and (5) give \(q_u(x)>0\) and the derivatives of \(u\mapsto q_u(x)\) and \(u\mapsto U_u(x)\); the previous step then shows that \(u\mapsto F(u,x)\) has derivative \(\varphi_u(x)\). \(\square\)

None of the hypotheses is a statement about the derivative of the integral itself. Domination is needed because \(E\) is unbounded and the densities need not be compactly supported.

steps.title: Divergence in coordinates and integration by parts
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(e_1,\dots,e_d\) be a fixed orthonormal basis of \(E\). For a vector field \(V:E o E\) the components are \(V_i(x)=\langle V(x),e_i angle\), and the divergence is

\[ abla\cdot V(x)=\sum_{i=1}^d\partial_iV_i(x),\qquad\partial_if(x)=Df(x)\,e_i,\]

where \(Df(x)\) is the Fréchet derivative. If \(V\) has Fréchet derivative \(A\) at \(x\), then \(V_i\) has derivative \(h\mapsto\langle Ah,e_i angle\), so \( abla\cdot V(x)=\sum_i\langle Ae_i,e_i angle=\operatorname{tr}A\). Components and divergence are linear in \(V\); in particular \((-V)_i=-V_i\) and \( abla\cdot(-V)=- abla\cdot V\).

For \(V:E o E\) and \(\psi:E o\mathbb R\), the no-boundary-flux condition requires that each component \(V_i\) is differentiable and that, for each \(i\), the three functions

\[(\partial_iV_i)\,\psi,\qquad V_i\,\partial_i\psi,\qquad V_i\,\psi\]

are Lebesgue integrable on \(E\). These are the hypotheses of Lebesgue integration by parts on \(E\); they replace the boundary terms that vanish on a bounded domain. The condition is unchanged when \(V\) is replaced by \(-V\).

Claim. Let \(\psi\) be differentiable and let \((V,\psi)\) satisfy the no-boundary-flux condition. Then \(x\mapsto\langle V(x), abla\psi(x) angle\) and \(x\mapsto abla\cdot V(x)\,\psi(x)\) are integrable, and

\[\int_E abla\cdot V\,\psi\,dx=-\int_E\langle V, abla\psi angle\,dx.\qquad(1)\]

Proof. Expanding in the orthonormal basis, \(\langle u,w angle=\sum_i\langle u,e_i angle\langle w,e_i angle\); with \(\langle abla\psi(x),e_i angle=D\psi(x)e_i=\partial_i\psi(x)\) this gives

\[\langle V(x), abla\psi(x) angle=\sum_iV_i(x)\,\partial_i\psi(x),\qquad abla\cdot V(x)\,\psi(x)=\sum_i\partial_iV_i(x)\,\psi(x).\]

Both are finite sums of integrable functions, hence integrable, and the integrals split into sums over \(i\). For each \(i\) we use Lebesgue integration by parts in the direction \(e_i\): if \(f,g:E o\mathbb R\) are differentiable and \(f\,\partial_ig\), \((\partial_if)\,g\) and \(fg\) are integrable, then \(\int f\,\partial_ig\,dx=-\int(\partial_if)\,g\,dx\). (On each line parallel to \(e_i\) this is the one-dimensional formula; integrability of \(fg\) forces the boundary values to vanish along a sequence of endpoints, and Fubini's theorem integrates over the lines.) With \(f=V_i\) and \(g=\psi\), the three integrability conditions are those of the no-boundary-flux condition, so \(\int V_i\,\partial_i\psi=-\int\partial_iV_i\,\psi\). Summing over \(i\) gives (1). \(\square\)

steps.title: The score pairing under a density law
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(q:E o\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable with \(q(x)>0\) for every \(x\), let \(V:E o E\), and let \((V,q)\) satisfy the no-boundary-flux condition. Let \(Q\) be the measure \(Q(dx)=q(x)\,dx\). Then \( abla\cdot V\) and \(\langle V, abla\log q angle\) are \(Q\)-integrable and

\[\int_E abla\cdot V\,dQ=-\int_E\langle V, abla\log q angle\,dQ.\]

Proof. For a measurable function \(f\), integrability of \(f\) with respect to \(Q\) is equivalent to Lebesgue integrability of \(qf\), and then \(\int f\,dQ=\int qf\,dx\); this is the definition of a measure with a density, valid because \(q\) is measurable (continuous) and nonnegative. Since \(q>0\) is differentiable, the chain rule gives \( abla\log q=q^{-1} abla q\), hence

\[q\,\langle V, abla\log q angle=\langle V, abla q angle.\]

By the previous step with \(\psi=q\), the functions \( abla\cdot V\,q\) and \(\langle V, abla q angle\) are Lebesgue integrable, and \(\int abla\cdot V\,q\,dx=-\int\langle V, abla q angle\,dx\). Translating back to \(Q\) with the identity above proves both integrability statements and the formula. \(\square\)

When \(V(x)=T(x)-x\) is a transport displacement and \(Q\) is a probability law, this is the identity that relates the divergence of the displacement to the score \( abla\log q\).

For a density \(q\) on a measure space \((X, u)\), a potential \(U:A imes X o\mathbb R\) and \(a\in A\), the parameter force is the Bochner integral

\[P(a)=\int_Xq(x)\, abla_aU(a,x)\, u(dx)\in A,\]

where \( abla_aU(a,x)\in A\) is the gradient of \(b\mapsto U(b,x)\) at \(a\), defined by \(\langle abla_aU(a,x),w angle=D_aU(a,x)[w]\).

  3. \(q^m_t>0\) everywhere, and \(q^m_t\) and \(U_m(p(t),\cdot)\) are continuously differentiable;
  4. \(q^m_t\,\nabla_aU_m(p(t),\cdot)\) is integrable;

LatentDiffusion/RegularTransport.lean.title: Displacement convexity of the free energy
LatentDiffusion/RegularTransport.lean.summary:
This section proves the strong geodesic convexity of the tilted free energy along displacement interpolations, the paper's Lemma C.4,.

The extra transport assumptions are Extra A4.

Let \(Z\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space of dimension \(d\), let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(Z\) (the initial law) and let \(T:Z\to Z\) be a transport map. The displacement interpolation is \(T_s(z)=(1-s)z+sT(z)\), \(s\in[0,1]\), and its law is the pushforward \(\mu_s=\mu\circ T_s^{-1}\). For one datum, a parameter interpolation \(p_s=(1-s)p_0+sp_1\) and a joint potential \(U(p,z)\), the free energy along the interpolation is

\[\mathcal F(s)=H(s)+\int_ZU(p_s,z)\,\mu_s(dz),\qquad H(s)=\int_Z\log\rho_s\,d\mu_s,\]

where \(\rho_s\) is the Lebesgue density of \(\mu_s\) and \(H\) is the negative Boltzmann entropy.

The extra transport assumptions are positive densities, positive eigenvalues of the Jacobian \(DT\) in an orthonormal eigenbasis, the change-of-variables formula \(\rho_s(T_s(z))=\rho_0(z)/\det\bigl((1-s)I+sDT(z)\bigr)\), and integrable logarithms; no convexity or transport inequality is among them.

If \(U\) is jointly \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, we prove

\[\mathcal F(s)\le(1-s)\mathcal F(0)+s\mathcal F(1)-\frac\lambda2s(1-s)\bigl(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+W_2(\mu_0,\mu_1)^2\bigr),\]

where \(W_2\) is the Wasserstein distance. The entropy part follows from concavity of \(\log\det\); the potential part from joint strong convexity. Consequences are a Talagrand-type quadratic growth at a minimizer and the tangent inequality used for the extended log-Sobolev inequality in the next section.

steps.title: The interpolated Jacobian and concavity of its logarithm
steps.body:
For real numbers \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d\) and \(s\in\mathbb R\) put

\[J(s)=\prod_{i=1}^d\bigl((1-s)+s\lambda_i\bigr).\]

If a linear map \(A\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\), then \((1-s)I+sA\) has the same eigenvectors with eigenvalues \((1-s)+s\lambda_i\), so \(J(s)=\det((1-s)I+sA)\).

Claim. Let \(\lambda_i>0\) for all \(i\) and \(s\in[0,1]\). Then

  1. \(J(s)>0\), \(J(0)=1\) and \(J(1)=\prod_i\lambda_i\);
  2. \(s\log J(1)\le\log J(s)\).

Proof. (1) If \(s=0\) every factor equals \(1\). If \(s>0\), every factor is the sum of \(1-s\ge0\) and \(s\lambda_i>0\), hence positive. A product of positive numbers is positive. The values at \(s=0\) and \(s=1\) are immediate.

(2) The logarithm is concave on \((0,\infty)\). For the points \(1\) and \(\lambda_i\) and the weights \(1-s\) and \(s\),

\[\log\bigl((1-s)\cdot1+s\lambda_i\bigr)\ge(1-s)\log1+s\log\lambda_i=s\log\lambda_i.\]

Since all factors are positive, the logarithm of each product is the sum of the logarithms, and summing over \(i\) gives \(\log J(s)\ge s\sum_i\log\lambda_i=s\log J(1)\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Regular displacement data
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\nu\) and \(\mu\) be measures on \(Z\) (in applications \(\nu\) is Lebesgue measure and \(\mu\) a probability measure). For a map \(T:Z\to Z\) the displacement interpolation is \(T_s(z)=(1-s)z+sT(z)\); thus \(T_0=\mathrm{id}\), \(T_1=T\), and \(T_s\) is measurable when \(T\) is. Regular displacement data consist of

  1. a measurable map \(T\);
  2. functions \(\rho_s:Z\to\mathbb R\), measurable and strictly positive for \(s\in[0,1]\), such that the pushforward of \(\mu\) under \(T_s\) has density \(\rho_s\) with respect to \(\nu\): \(\mu\circ T_s^{-1}=\rho_s\,\nu\);
  3. for each \(z\), an orthonormal basis \((b_i(z))_{i=1}^d\) of \(Z\) and positive numbers \(\lambda_i(z)\) such that \(T\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(z\) with derivative \(DT(z)\) satisfying \(DT(z)b_i(z)=\lambda_i(z)b_i(z)\);
  4. the change-of-variables formula: for \(s\in[0,1]\) and every \(z\), \[\rho_s(T_s(z))=\frac{\rho_0(z)}{J_z(s)},\qquad J_z(s)=\prod_i\bigl((1-s)+s\lambda_i(z)\bigr);\]
  5. for \(s\in[0,1]\), \(\mu\)-integrability of \(z\mapsto\log\rho_s(T_s(z))\).

Condition (4) is the local conservation of mass for the smooth positive-Jacobian map \(T_s\); it is an assumption on the data, not an entropy inequality. Arbitrary pairs of probability laws need not admit such data, which is why they form the explicit hypothesis Extra A4.

Claim. (1) \(\det DT(z)=J_z(1)=\prod_i\lambda_i(z)\) and \(\operatorname{tr}DT(z)=\sum_i\lambda_i(z)\). (2) The law \(\mu_s=\mu\circ T_s^{-1}\) satisfies \(\mu_0=\mu\) and \(\mu_1=\mu\circ T^{-1}\), and it is a probability measure for every \(s\) if \(\mu\) is.

Proof. (1) In the orthonormal basis \((b_i(z))\) the matrix of \(DT(z)\) is diagonal with entries \(\lambda_i(z)\), because \(DT(z)b_j=\lambda_jb_j\). The determinant and the trace are independent of the basis; for a diagonal matrix they are the product and the sum of the diagonal entries. (2) \(T_0\) is the identity and \(T_1=T\). The pushforward of a probability measure by a measurable map has total mass \(\mu(T_s^{-1}(Z))=\mu(Z)=1\). \(\square\)

Part (1) checks that the product in (4) is the Jacobian determinant of the actual map \(T\), and the trace formula is used for the divergence of the displacement \(T-\mathrm{id}\).

steps.title: Displacement convexity of the entropy
steps.body:
The entropy at time \(s\) is \(H(s)=\int\log\rho_s\,d\mu_s\). Since \(\mu_s\) has density \(\rho_s\), this is \(\int\rho_s\log\rho_s\,d\nu\), the negative Boltzmann entropy of \(\mu_s\).

Claim. For regular displacement data and \(s\in[0,1]\),

  1. for every \(z\), \(\log\rho_s(T_s(z))\le(1-s)\log\rho_0(z)+s\log\rho_1(T(z))\);
  2. \(H(s)=\int\log\rho_s(T_s(z))\,\mu(dz)\);
  3. \(H(s)\le(1-s)H(0)+sH(1)\).

Proof. (1) By the change-of-variables formula at times \(s\) and \(1\) (with \(T_1=T\)),

\[\log\rho_s(T_s(z))=\log\rho_0(z)-\log J_z(s),\qquad\log\rho_1(T(z))=\log\rho_0(z)-\log J_z(1),\]

where the logarithms of quotients split because \(\rho_0(z)>0\) and \(J_z(s),J_z(1)>0\) (first step). The first step gives \(\log J_z(s)\ge s\log J_z(1)\), hence

\[\log\rho_s(T_s(z))\le\log\rho_0(z)-s\log J_z(1)=(1-s)\log\rho_0(z)+s\bigl(\log\rho_0(z)-\log J_z(1)\bigr),\]

which is (1).

(2) For a measurable map \(\Phi\) and a measurable function \(f\), \(\int f\,d(\mu\circ\Phi^{-1})=\int f\circ\Phi\,d\mu\) (change of variables for pushforward measures). Apply it with \(\Phi=T_s\) and \(f=\log\rho_s\), which is measurable because \(\rho_s\) is.

(3) By (2), \(H(s)\), \(H(0)\) and \(H(1)\) are the \(\mu\)-integrals of \(\log\rho_s\circ T_s\), \(\log\rho_0\) and \(\log\rho_1\circ T\); these three functions are \(\mu\)-integrable by condition (5) at \(s\), \(0\) and \(1\). Integrating the pointwise inequality (1) against \(\mu\) and using linearity and monotonicity of the integral gives (3). \(\square\)

No convexity hypothesis on the laws is used: displacement convexity of the entropy is a consequence of the change-of-variables formula and the concavity of \(\log\det\) on positive definite spectra.

steps.title: Strong convexity of the potential energy along the displacement
steps.body:
Let \(P\) be a complete real inner product space of parameters, and give \(P\times Z\) the Euclidean product norm \(\|(p,z)\|^2=\|p\|^2+\|z\|^2\). For \(p_0,p_1\in P\) put \(p_s=(1-s)p_0+sp_1\), and for \(U:P\times Z\to\mathbb R\) define the free energy of one datum along the interpolation by \(\mathcal F(s)=H(s)+\int U(p_s,\cdot)\,d\mu_s\). For a square-integrable vector function \(X\) write \(\|X\|_{L^2(\mu)}=(\int\|X\|^2d\mu)^{1/2}\); the identity \(\|X\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2=\int\|X\|^2\,d\mu\) holds by definition of this norm.

Claim. Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure, \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), and let \(U\) be \(\lambda\)-strongly convex on \(P\times Z\). Assume that \(U(p,\cdot)\) is measurable for every \(p\), that \(z\mapsto U(p_s,T_s(z))\) is \(\mu\)-integrable for every \(s\in[0,1]\), and that \(z\mapsto z-T(z)\) is square integrable under \(\mu\). Then for \(s\in[0,1]\),

\[\begin{aligned}\int U(p_s,\cdot)\,d\mu_s\le{}&(1-s)\int U(p_0,z)\,\mu(dz)+s\int U(p_1,T(z))\,\mu(dz)\\&-\frac\lambda2s(1-s)\bigl(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+\|\mathrm{id}-T\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2\bigr).\end{aligned}\]

Proof. Fix \(z\). The points \((p_0,z)\) and \((p_1,T(z))\) have the convex combination \((1-s)(p_0,z)+s(p_1,T(z))=(p_s,T_s(z))\) and squared distance \(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+\|z-T(z)\|^2\). Strong convexity with the weights \(1-s\) and \(s\) gives

\[U(p_s,T_s(z))\le(1-s)U(p_0,z)+sU(p_1,T(z))-\frac\lambda2s(1-s)\bigl(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+\|z-T(z)\|^2\bigr).\]

All functions of \(z\) on both sides are \(\mu\)-integrable: the potential terms by hypothesis at \(s\), \(0\) and \(1\), the constant because \(\mu\) is finite, and \(\|z-T(z)\|^2\) by square integrability. Integrating against \(\mu\) and using \(\mu(Z)=1\) and \(\int\|z-T(z)\|^2d\mu=\|\mathrm{id}-T\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2\) gives the claim, after writing \(\int U(p_s,\cdot)\,d\mu_s=\int U(p_s,T_s(z))\,\mu(dz)\) by the pushforward formula. \(\square\)

steps.title: Strong displacement convexity of the free energy

Wasserstein distance. For probability measures \(\mu,\eta\) on \(Z\), a coupling is a probability measure \(\gamma\) on \(Z\times Z\) with marginals \(\mu\) and \(\eta\), and

\[W_2(\mu,\eta)=\inf_\gamma\Bigl(\int\|x-y\|^2\,\gamma(dx,dy)\Bigr)^{1/2}\in[0,\infty].\]

By (2), \(c\bigl(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+W_2(\mu,\mu_1)^2\bigr)\le c\bigl(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+\|\mathrm{id}-T\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2\bigr)\), so the right side of (1) is at most the right side of (3), and (3) follows from (1). \(\square\)

steps.title: The tangent inequality and the Cauchy–Schwarz bound
steps.body:
Claim 1. Let \(H\) be a real normed space, \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), and \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) \(\lambda\)-strongly convex. If \(U\) has Fréchet derivative \(A\) at \(x\), then for every \(y\in H\),

\[U(x)+A(y-x)+\frac\lambda2\|x-y\|^2\le U(y).\]

Proof. Put \(f(s)=U(x+s(y-x))\). By the chain rule \(f\) is differentiable at \(0\) with \(f'(0)=A(y-x)\). Since \(x+s(y-x)=(1-s)x+sy\), strong convexity gives \(f(s)\le(1-s)f(0)+sU(y)-\frac\lambda2s(1-s)\|x-y\|^2\) for \(s\in[0,1]\). For \(0<s<1\) this is equivalent to

\[\frac{f(s)-f(0)}s\le U(y)-f(0)-\frac\lambda2(1-s)\|x-y\|^2.\]

As \(s\downarrow0\) the left side tends to \(f'(0)\) and the right side to \(U(y)-U(x)-\frac\lambda2\|x-y\|^2\); limits preserve the inequality. \(\square\)

Claim 2. Let \(Q\) be a measure and let \(A,B\) be square-integrable functions with values in a real inner product space. Then \(\int\langle A,B\rangle\,dQ\le\|A\|_{L^2(Q)}\|B\|_{L^2(Q)}\).

Proof. The integral is the inner product of \(A\) and \(B\) in the Hilbert space \(L^2(Q)\), and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds it by the product of the norms. \(\square\)

LatentDiffusion/RegularTransportFirstOrd.title: The extended log-Sobolev and Talagrand inequalities
LatentDiffusion/RegularTransportFirstOrd.summary:
This section proves the two functional inequalities that drive the convergence of the classical flow: the extended log-Sobolev inequality (the paper's Theorem stating that strong log-concavity implies extended LSI) and a Talagrand-type quadratic growth inequality, both for the normalized free energy of \(M\) data. The setting is that of the previous section, now for each datum \(m\): a probability law \(Q_m\) on \(Z\) with positive continuously differentiable density \(\rho_{m}\), regular displacement data \(T_m\) from \(Q_m\), and a jointly \(\lambda\)-strongly convex potential \(U_m\) on \(P\times Z\). With \(p_0\) the current parameter, \(p_1\) the target parameter and \(\mathcal F_m\) the free energy of datum \(m\) along the displacement, put \(\mathcal F=M^{-1}\sum_m\mathcal F_m\), and define

\[\begin{aligned}G&=\frac1M\sum_m\int\nabla_pU_m(p_0,z)\,Q_m(dz),\\ S_m&=\nabla_z\bigl(\log\rho_m+U_m(p_0,\cdot)\bigr),\\I&=\|G\|^2+\frac1M\sum_m\int\|S_m\|^2\,dQ_m.\end{aligned}\]

The main result is \(2\lambda\bigl(\mathcal F(0)-\mathcal F(1)\bigr)\le I\). In the convergence theorem \(\mathcal F(0)\) is the free energy of the current state and \(\mathcal F(1)\) that of the posterior optimizer, so this is \(2\lambda(F-F_\star)\le I\). The proof sums two tangent inequalities, one for the entropy (from the Jacobian formula, \(\log x\le x-1\) and integration by parts) and one for the potential (from strong convexity), and then completes a square in which the parameter forces are averaged over the data before the norm is squared. The last step proves \(\frac\lambda2d^2\le\mathcal F(0)-\mathcal F(1)\) when the endpoint minimizes \(\mathcal F\) along the displacement, where \(d\) is the normalized product distance. No first-order transport inequality or log-Sobolev inequality is assumed.

steps.title: The entropy tangent inequality
steps.body:
Let \(D\) be regular displacement data from a probability law \(\mu\) on \(Z\), with Lebesgue measure as reference: transport \(T\), interpolation \(T_s\), densities \(\rho_s\), Jacobian eigenvalues \(\lambda_i(z)>0\), and entropies \(H(s)=\int\log\rho_s\,d\mu_s=\int\log\rho_s(T_s(z))\,\mu(dz)\).

Claim. (1) \(\mu(dz)=\rho_0(z)\,dz\). (2) The displacement \(V(z)=T(z)-z\) has divergence \(\nabla\cdot V(z)=\sum_i(\lambda_i(z)-1)\). (3) For every \(z\), \(\log\rho_0(z)-\sum_i(\lambda_i(z)-1)\le\log\rho_1(T(z))\). (4) If moreover \(\rho_0\) is continuously differentiable and \((V,\rho_0)\) satisfies the no-boundary-flux condition, then

\[\int_Z\langle T(z)-z,\nabla\log\rho_0(z)\rangle\,\mu(dz)\le H(1)-H(0).\]

Proof. (1) is the law condition at \(s=0\), where \(T_0\) is the identity. (2) \(V\) has derivative \(DT(z)-I\) at \(z\), so its divergence is \(\operatorname{tr}(DT(z)-I)\). In the orthonormal eigenbasis \((b_i(z))\), \(\langle(DT(z)-I)b_i,b_i\rangle=\lambda_i(z)-1\), and the trace is the sum of these numbers.

(3) By the change-of-variables formula at \(s=1\), \(\rho_1(T(z))=\rho_0(z)/\prod_i\lambda_i(z)\), so \(\log\rho_1(T(z))=\log\rho_0(z)-\sum_i\log\lambda_i(z)\). The inequality \(\log x\le x-1\) for \(x>0\) gives \(\sum_i\log\lambda_i(z)\le\sum_i(\lambda_i(z)-1)\), which proves (3).

(4) By (1) and the score pairing of the flow-calculus section, applied with \(q=\rho_0\) and \(V=T-\mathrm{id}\), both \(\nabla\cdot V\) and \(\langle V,\nabla\log\rho_0\rangle\) are \(\mu\)-integrable and

\[\int\langle T(z)-z,\nabla\log\rho_0(z)\rangle\,\mu(dz)=-\int\nabla\cdot V\,d\mu=-\int\sum_i(\lambda_i-1)\,d\mu,\]

using (2). The functions \(\log\rho_0\) and \(\log\rho_1\circ T\) are \(\mu\)-integrable by the extra transport assumptions. Integrating (3) against \(\mu\) gives \(H(0)-\int\sum_i(\lambda_i-1)\,d\mu\le H(1)\), which is (4) after substituting the displayed identity. \(\square\)

steps.body:
The joint space \(P\times Z\) carries the Euclidean product norm. The displacement field of the transport and of the parameter move \(p_0\to p_1\) is \(\Delta(z)=(p_1-p_0,\,T(z)-z)\in P\times Z\).

\[\int\langle G(z),\Delta(z)\rangle\,\mu(dz)+\frac\lambda2\bigl(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+\|\mathrm{id}-T\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2\bigr)\le\int U(p_1,T(z))\,\mu(dz)-\int U(p_0,z)\,\mu(dz).\]

steps.title: The free-energy tangent inequality
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mathcal F(s)=H(s)+\int U(p_s,\cdot)\,d\mu_s\) be the free energy of one datum along the displacement. Assume the hypotheses of the two previous steps, together with measurability of \(U(p,\cdot)\) for every \(p\). Then

\[\int\langle G,\Delta\rangle\,d\mu+\int\langle T(z)-z,\nabla\log\rho_0(z)\rangle\,\mu(dz)+\frac\lambda2\bigl(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+\|\mathrm{id}-T\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2\bigr)\le\mathcal F(1)-\mathcal F(0).\]

Proof. Since \(\mu_0=\mu\), \(p_0\) is the parameter at \(s=0\), and \(\int U(p_1,\cdot)\,d\mu_1=\int U(p_1,T(z))\,\mu(dz)\) by the pushforward formula,

\[\mathcal F(1)-\mathcal F(0)=H(1)-H(0)+\int U(p_1,T(z))\,\mu(dz)-\int U(p_0,z)\,\mu(dz).\]

The entropy tangent inequality bounds \(H(1)-H(0)\) from below and the potential tangent inequality bounds the potential difference from below; adding the two lower bounds gives the claim. \(\square\)

steps.title: Completing the square over the data
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(M\ge1\), \(\lambda>0\), \(w\in P\), and for \(m=1,\dots,M\) let \(\gamma_m,\kappa_m,b_m,c_m\in\mathbb R\) and \(g_m\in P\) satisfy

\[\gamma_m+\langle g_m,w\rangle+\kappa_m+\frac\lambda2\bigl(\|w\|^2+c_m^2\bigr)\le0\qquad\text{and}\qquad-\kappa_m\le b_mc_m.\]

Then

\[2\lambda\cdot\frac1M\sum_m\gamma_m\le\Bigl\|\frac1M\sum_mg_m\Bigr\|^2+\frac1M\sum_mb_m^2.\]

Proof. Multiply the first hypothesis by \(2\lambda>0\) and use the second:

\[2\lambda\gamma_m\le-2\lambda\langle g_m,w\rangle-\lambda^2\|w\|^2+\bigl(2\lambda b_mc_m-\lambda^2c_m^2\bigr)\le-2\lambda\langle g_m,w\rangle-\lambda^2\|w\|^2+b_m^2,\]

where the last inequality is \((b_m-\lambda c_m)^2\ge0\). Average over \(m\) and write \(\bar g=M^{-1}\sum_mg_m\); since \(M^{-1}\cdot M=1\),

\[2\lambda\cdot\frac1M\sum_m\gamma_m\le-2\lambda\langle\bar g,w\rangle-\lambda^2\|w\|^2+\frac1M\sum_mb_m^2.\]

Finally \(0\le\|\bar g+\lambda w\|^2=\|\bar g\|^2+2\lambda\langle\bar g,w\rangle+\lambda^2\|w\|^2\), so \(-2\lambda\langle\bar g,w\rangle-\lambda^2\|w\|^2\le\|\bar g\|^2\). \(\square\)

The parameter vectors are averaged before the square is completed. Averaging \(M\) separate one-datum inequalities would produce \(M^{-1}\sum_m\|g_m\|^2\), which is larger than \(\|\bar g\|^2\) and is not the Fisher information of the paper.

steps.title: Transport assumptions for the data set
steps.body:
Definition. Fix parameters \(p_0,p_1\in P\), \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) and \(M\) data. The transport hypotheses combine the paper's strong convexity assumption with the extra density, integrability and map assumptions Extra A4.

For each datum \(m\), the extra conditions are the density/map data and integrability requirements below; strong convexity is assumption A3. Supply:

  1. a probability law \(Q_m\) on \(Z\) and regular displacement data \(D_m\) from \(Q_m\) with Lebesgue reference measure (transport \(T_m\), densities \(\rho_{m,s}\));
  2. a potential \(U_m:P\times Z\to\mathbb R\) that is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex on \(P\times Z\), with \(U_m(p,\cdot)\) measurable for every \(p\);
  3. integrability under \(Q_m\) of \(U_m(p_0,\cdot)\), of \(z\mapsto U_m(p_1,T_m(z))\) and of \(z\mapsto U_m(p_s,T_{m,s}(z))\) for \(s\in[0,1]\);
  4. gradients \(G_m(z)\) of \(U_m\) at \((p_0,z)\), with \(G_m\) square integrable under \(Q_m\);
  5. square integrability of \(z\mapsto z-T_m(z)\) and of \(\nabla\log\rho_{m,0}\) under \(Q_m\);
  6. continuous differentiability of \(\rho_{m,0}\), and the no-boundary-flux condition for \((T_m-\mathrm{id},\rho_{m,0})\).

From these data define the averaged free energy \(\mathcal F(s)=M^{-1}\sum_m\mathcal F_m(s)\), the parameter force \(G=M^{-1}\sum_m\int G_{m,P}\,dQ_m\), the latent scores \(S_m=G_{m,Z}+\nabla\log\rho_{m,0}\), and the Fisher information

\[I=\|G\|^2+\frac1M\sum_m\int\|S_m\|^2\,dQ_m.\]

Since \(G_{m,Z}(z)\) is the latent component of the gradient of \(U_m\) at \((p_0,z)\), \(S_m=\nabla_z(\log\rho_{m,0}+U_m(p_0,\cdot))\) is the latent score of the summary.

Claim. Each \(S_m\) is square integrable under \(Q_m\).

Proof. \(G_{m,Z}\) is square integrable by the previous step, \(\nabla\log\rho_{m,0}\) by (5), and a sum of square-integrable functions is square integrable. \(\square\)

steps.title: The extended log-Sobolev inequality
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(M\ge1\), \(\lambda>0\), and assume the transport hypotheses for the data set. Then

\[2\lambda\bigl(\mathcal F(0)-\mathcal F(1)\bigr)\le I.\]

Proof. For each datum \(m\) put

\[\begin{aligned}\gamma_m&=\mathcal F_m(0)-\mathcal F_m(1),&g_m&=\int G_{m,P}\,dQ_m,\\\kappa_m&=\int\langle S_m,T_m-\mathrm{id}\rangle\,dQ_m,\\b_m&=\|S_m\|_{L^2(Q_m)},&c_m&=\|\mathrm{id}-T_m\|_{L^2(Q_m)}.\end{aligned}\]

Tangent inequality. The free-energy tangent inequality for datum \(m\), with its left side rewritten by the splitting step, reads

\[\langle g_m,p_1-p_0\rangle+\kappa_m+\frac\lambda2\bigl(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+c_m^2\bigr)\le\mathcal F_m(1)-\mathcal F_m(0),\]

that is, \(\gamma_m+\langle g_m,w\rangle+\kappa_m+\frac\lambda2(\|w\|^2+c_m^2)\le0\) with \(w=p_1-p_0\), since \(\|p_0-p_1\|=\|w\|\).

Pairing bound. By the Cauchy-Schwarz bound of the previous section applied to \(-S_m\) and \(T_m-\mathrm{id}\), \(-\kappa_m=\int\langle-S_m,T_m-\mathrm{id}\rangle\,dQ_m\le b_mc_m\); here \(\|T_m-\mathrm{id}\|_{L^2}=\|\mathrm{id}-T_m\|_{L^2}\).

Completion of the square. The previous step gives \(2\lambda M^{-1}\sum_m\gamma_m\le\|M^{-1}\sum_mg_m\|^2+M^{-1}\sum_mb_m^2\). The left side is \(2\lambda(\mathcal F(0)-\mathcal F(1))\). On the right, \(M^{-1}\sum_mg_m=G\) and \(b_m^2=\int\|S_m\|^2\,dQ_m\), so the right side is \(I\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Displacement convexity over the data set and the Talagrand inequality
steps.body:
The normalized product distance between \((p_0,(Q_m)_m)\) and \((p_1,(Q_m\circ T_m^{-1})_m)\) is given by

\[d^2=\|p_0-p_1\|^2+\frac1M\sum_mW_2\bigl(Q_m,Q_m\circ T_m^{-1}\bigr)^2\ge0.\]

Claim. Let \(M\ge1\) and \(\lambda\ge0\). (1) For every \(s\in[0,1]\),

\[\mathcal F(s)\le(1-s)\mathcal F(0)+s\mathcal F(1)-\frac\lambda2s(1-s)\,d^2.\]

(2) If the endpoint minimizes along the displacement, \(\mathcal F(1)\le\mathcal F(s)\) for all \(s\in[0,1]\), then

\[\frac\lambda2\,d^2\le\mathcal F(0)-\mathcal F(1).\]

Proof. (1) For each \(m\), the strong displacement convexity of the previous section gives the inequality for \(\mathcal F_m\) with the bracket \(\|p_0-p_1\|^2+W_2(Q_m,Q_m\circ T_m^{-1})^2\). Averaging over \(m\) and using \(M^{-1}\sum_m\|p_0-p_1\|^2=\|p_0-p_1\|^2\) (here \(M\ge1\)) gives (1).

(2) Put \(f(s)=\mathcal F(1-s)\) for \(s\in[0,1]\). Then \(f(0)=\mathcal F(1)\le f(s)\) by hypothesis, and (1) at the time \(1-s\in[0,1]\) gives

\[f(s)\le s\,\mathcal F(0)+(1-s)\mathcal F(1)-\frac\lambda2(1-s)s\,d^2=(1-s)f(0)+s\,\mathcal F(0)-\frac\lambda2s(1-s)\,d^2.\]

The elementary quadratic-growth fact of the previous section (if \(f(0)\le f(s)\le(1-s)f(0)+sf_1-\frac\lambda2s(1-s)D^2\) on \([0,1]\), then \(\frac\lambda2D^2\le f_1-f(0)\)) applies with \(f_1=\mathcal F(0)\) and \(D=d\). \(\square\)

In the convergence theorem, the endpoint is the posterior optimizer, whose minimality along the displacement follows from the Gibbs variational principle; (2) then bounds the distance to the optimizer by the free-energy gap.

LatentDiffusion/RegularConvergence.lean.title: Exponential convergence of the classical flow
LatentDiffusion/RegularConvergence.lean.summary:
This section proves the paper's continuous-time convergence theorem (Theorem 3.1 and its appendix form, Theorem C.12) for classical solutions of the joint gradient flow. The flow consists of a parameter path \(a_t\) and positive densities \(q_t^1,\dots,q_t^M\) solving

\[\dot a_t=-\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\int\nabla_aU_m(a_t,z)\,q_t^m(z)\,dz,\qquad\partial_tq_t^m=\nabla\cdot\bigl(q_t^m\nabla(\log q_t^m+U_m(a_t,\cdot))\bigr),\]

The flow also satisfies extra assumptions Extra A1–Extra A4: local domination, integrable spatial tails, and, at each time, regular displacement data from the current laws to the laws of a fixed comparison state \(a_\star\).

Existence of such a classical solution is not constructed; the estimates hold for every solution in this class. Write \(E(t)=\mathcal E(a_t,q_t)-\mathcal E(a_\star,q_\star)\) for the energy gap to the comparison state and \(d_t\) for the normalized product distance

\[d_t^2=\|a_t-a_\star\|^2+\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^MW_2(q_t^m,\pi_{a_\star}^m)^2.\]

When \(a_\star\) maximizes the evidence and the comparison densities are the posteriors \(\pi_{a_\star}^m\), we prove

\[d_t\le\sqrt{\frac{2E(t)}\lambda}\le\sqrt{\frac{2E(0)}\lambda}\,e^{-\lambda t},\qquad\|a_t-a_\star\|\le\sqrt{\frac{2E(0)}\lambda}\,e^{-\lambda t}\qquad(t\ge0).\]

The ingredients are the de Bruijn identity \(E'=-I\), the extended log-Sobolev inequality \(2\lambda E\le I\), Grönwall's inequality, and the Talagrand inequality \(\frac\lambda2d_t^2\le E(t)\), whose hypothesis (minimality of the posterior state) follows from the Gibbs variational principle. The final theorem constructs \(a_\star\) as the unique maximizer of the evidence of the original potentials, so the only remaining hypotheses are the extra assumptions defining the flow.

steps.title: The Gibbs variational lower bound
steps.body:
Claim 1. If \(q:Z\to\mathbb R\) is measurable and nonnegative and \(Q(dz)=q(z)\,dz\), then \(\int f\,dQ=\int q\,f\,dz\) for every function \(f\) with values in a normed space, with both sides read as Bochner integrals (equal to \(0\) for nonintegrable functions).

Claim 2. Let \(Q\) be a probability law with a measurable, strictly positive Lebesgue density \(q\). Let \(V:Z\to\mathbb R\) be such that \(e^{-V}\) is integrable with \(Z_V=\int e^{-V}dz>0\), and such that \(\log q\) and \(V\) are \(Q\)-integrable. Then

\[-\log Z_V\le\int\log q\,dQ+\int V\,dQ.\]

Proof. Claim 1 is the definition of the integral against a measure with density, together with the fact that \(q\) is real and nonnegative. For Claim 2, define \(r(z)=\dfrac{e^{-V(z)}/Z_V}{q(z)}>0\), so that \(q\,r=e^{-V}/Z_V\). By Claim 1, \(r\) is \(Q\)-integrable if and only if \(qr\) is Lebesgue integrable, which holds, and \(\int r\,dQ=\int e^{-V}dz/Z_V=1\).

For \(x>0\), \(\log x\le x-1\). With \(x=r(z)\) and \(\log r=-V-\log Z_V-\log q\) this gives, for every \(z\),

\[1-r(z)\le\log q(z)+V(z)+\log Z_V.\]

Both sides are \(Q\)-integrable. Integrating against the probability measure \(Q\) gives \(1-1\le\int\log q\,dQ+\int V\,dQ+\log Z_V\). \(\square\)

Claim 2 is the nonnegativity of the relative entropy of \(Q\) with respect to the Gibbs law \(e^{-V}dz/Z_V\), proved directly from the pointwise inequality.

(4) Under the hypotheses of (2) and (3), if \(b\) maximizes \(\ell\), then \(\mathcal F(1)\le\mathcal F(s)\) for every \(s\in[0,1]\).

Proof. (1) By the pushforward formula, integrability of \(f\) under \(\mu_{m,s}=Q_m\circ T_{m,s}^{-1}\) is integrability of \(f\circ T_{m,s}\) under \(Q_m\); for \(f=\log\rho_{m,s}\) and \(f=U_m(p_s,\cdot)\) this is one of the extra transport assumptions.

\[-\log\int e^{-U_m(p_s,z)}dz\le\int\log\rho_{m,s}\,d\mu_{m,s}+\int U_m(p_s,\cdot)\,d\mu_{m,s}=\mathcal F_m(s).\]

Averaging over \(m\) gives \(-\ell(p_s)\le\mathcal F(s)\).

(3) At \(s=1\), \(p_1=b\) and \(\log\rho_{m,1}(z)+U_m(b,z)=-\log\int e^{-U_m(b,w)}dw\) is constant in \(z\). Its integral against the probability measure \(\mu_{m,1}\) is the same constant, so \(\mathcal F_m(1)=-\log\int e^{-U_m(b,w)}dw\), and averaging gives \(\mathcal F(1)=-\ell(b)\).

(4) By (3), maximality of \(b\) and (2): \(\mathcal F(1)=-\ell(b)\le-\ell(p_s)\le\mathcal F(s)\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Classical flows
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(A\) be a complete real inner product space of parameters, \(Z\) a finite-dimensional latent space, \(U_m:A\times Z\to\mathbb R\) potentials, \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) and \(a_\star\in A\) a comparison parameter. A classical flow consists of a parameter path \(a_t\) with derivatives \(\dot a_t\), densities \(q_t^m\) with rates \(\dot q_t^m\), comparison densities \(q_\star^m\), and, for every time \(t\), the transport assumptions for the data set from \((a_t,(q_t^m\,dz)_m)\) to \(a_\star\), such that:

  1. the data at time \(t\) use the potentials \(U_m\), start from the densities \(q_t^m\) and end at the densities \(q_\star^m\);
  2. \(a\) has derivative \(\dot a_t\) at every \(t\), and \(b\mapsto U_m(b,z)\) is differentiable everywhere;
  3. \(q_t^m>0\), and \(q_t^m\) and \(U_m(a_t,\cdot)\) are continuously differentiable;
  4. the gradient fields supplied by the extra transport assumptions at time \(t\) are the actual gradients: parameter component \(\nabla_aU_m(a_t,z)\) and latent component \(\nabla_zU_m(a_t,z)\);
  5. \(q_t^m\nabla_aU_m(a_t,\cdot)\) is integrable, and local domination holds at every \(t\) for the energy integrand;
  6. for \(t\ge0\), the parameter equation \(\dot a_t=-G(a_t,q_t)\) and the Fokker–Planck equations \(\dot q_t^m=\nabla\cdot(q_t^m\nabla(\log q_t^m+U_m(a_t,\cdot)))\) almost everywhere;
  7. the no-boundary-flux condition for the Fokker–Planck flux and the test \(\log q_t^m+U_m(a_t,\cdot)+1\), at every \(t\).

With \(\mathcal E\) and \(I\) of the flow-calculus section, define the energy \(\mathcal E(t)=\mathcal E(a_t,q_t)\), the Fisher information \(I(t)=I(a_t,q_t)\), the target energy \(\mathcal E_\star=\mathcal E(a_\star,q_\star)\), and the evidence \(\ell(a)=M^{-1}\sum_m\log\int e^{-U_m(a,z)}dz\).

All conditions concern densities, derivatives, integrability and the equations themselves. Neither the energy identity, nor a log-Sobolev or transport inequality, nor a convergence estimate is a condition.

steps.title: Identification of energies and Fisher information
steps.body:
For a classical flow and a time \(t\), let \(\mathcal F^{(t)}\), \(G^{(t)}\), \(S^{(t)}_m\), \(I^{(t)}\) and \(d_t^2\) denote the averaged free energy, parameter force, latent scores, Fisher information and squared distance under the extra transport assumptions at time \(t\) (previous section).

Claim. For every \(t\):

  1. \(\mathcal F^{(t)}(0)=\mathcal E(t)\) and \(\mathcal F^{(t)}(1)=\mathcal E_\star\);
  2. the endpoint law of datum \(m\) is \(q_\star^m(z)\,dz\); if \(q_\star^m=e^{-U_m(a_\star,\cdot)}/\int e^{-U_m(a_\star,w)}dw\), it is the posterior \(\pi_{a_\star}^m\), and then \(d_t^2=\|a_t-a_\star\|^2+M^{-1}\sum_mW_2(q_t^m\,dz,\pi^m_{a_\star})^2\);
  3. \(G^{(t)}=G(a_t,q_t)\), \(S^{(t)}_m=\nabla(\log q_t^m+U_m(a_t,\cdot))\), and \(I^{(t)}=I(t)\).

Proof. (1) At \(s=0\) the law of datum \(m\) is \(q_t^m\,dz\) and the parameter is \(a_t\). Hence \(\mathcal F^{(t)}_m(0)=\int\log q_t^m\,dQ_m+\int U_m(a_t,\cdot)\,dQ_m\); both functions are integrable by the extra transport assumptions, so the sum of the integrals is the integral of the sum, and by Claim 1 of the first step it equals \(\int q_t^m(\log q_t^m+U_m(a_t,\cdot))\,dz\). Averaging gives \(\mathcal E(t)\). The same computation at \(s=1\), with the law \(q_\star^m\,dz\) and the parameter \(a_\star\), gives \(\mathcal E_\star\).

(2) The first statement is the law condition at \(s=1\); the second substitutes the formula for \(q_\star^m\); the third inserts it into the definition of the distance.

(3) A gradient is unique: the gradient field of the data has, by condition (4) of the definition, the actual gradients as components. Hence \(\int G_{m,P}\,dQ_m=\int q_t^m\nabla_aU_m(a_t,\cdot)\,dz\) by Claim 1, and averaging gives \(G(a_t,q_t)\). Since \(q_t^m>0\) is continuously differentiable, \(\log q_t^m\) is differentiable and \(\nabla(\log q_t^m+U_m(a_t,\cdot))=\nabla\log q_t^m+\nabla_zU_m(a_t,\cdot)=S^{(t)}_m\). Inserting both identities into the definition of \(I^{(t)}\) and converting the \(Q_m\)-integrals by Claim 1 gives \(I(t)\). \(\square\)

steps.body:
Claim. (1) For \(t\ge0\), the energy is differentiable at \(t\) and \(\mathcal E'(t)=-I(t)\). (2) If \(M\ge1\) and \(\lambda>0\), then for every \(t\), \(2\lambda\bigl(\mathcal E(t)-\mathcal F^{(t)}(1)\bigr)\le I(t)\).

Proof. (1) The de Bruijn identity of the flow-calculus section requires local domination, differentiability of the parameter path and of the potentials in the parameter, positivity and continuous differentiability of \(q_t^m\) and \(U_m(a_t,\cdot)\), integrability of \(q_t^m\nabla_aU_m(a_t,\cdot)\), the parameter equation, the Fokker–Planck equations and the no-boundary-flux conditions. These are conditions (2), (3), (5), (6) and (7) of a classical flow; the equations hold because \(t\ge0\). Its conclusion is \(\mathcal E'(t)=-I(t)\).

(2) The extended log-Sobolev inequality of the previous section, under the extra transport assumptions at time \(t\), gives \(2\lambda(\mathcal F^{(t)}(0)-\mathcal F^{(t)}(1))\le I^{(t)}\). By the previous step, \(\mathcal F^{(t)}(0)=\mathcal E(t)\) and \(I^{(t)}=I(t)\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Exponential decay of the energy gap
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(M\ge1\), \(\lambda>0\) and \(T\ge0\). For every \(t\in[0,T]\),

\[\mathcal E(t)-\mathcal E_\star\le\bigl(\mathcal E(0)-\mathcal E_\star\bigr)e^{-2\lambda t}.\]

Proof. Put \(E(u)=\mathcal E(u)-\mathcal E_\star\). By the previous step, \(E\) is differentiable at every \(u\ge0\) with \(E'(u)=-I(u)\); in particular \(E\) is continuous on \([0,T]\). By the extended log-Sobolev inequality and \(\mathcal F^{(u)}(1)=\mathcal E_\star\),

\[E'(u)=-I(u)\le-2\lambda E(u)\qquad(u\ge0).\]

We use Grönwall's inequality in the following form: if \(f\) is continuous on \([0,T]\), has at every \(u\in[0,T)\) a right derivative \(f'(u)\) with \(f'(u)\le Kf(u)\), and \(f(0)\le\delta\), then \(f(t)\le\delta e^{Kt}\) for \(t\in[0,T]\). (One proof compares \(f\) with \(\delta e^{K t}+\varepsilon'(e^{Kt}-1)/K\) for \(\varepsilon'>0\): at a first time where \(f\) would exceed it, the right derivatives would contradict the strict inequality; then \(\varepsilon'\downarrow0\).) With \(f=E\), \(K=-2\lambda\) and \(\delta=E(0)\) we obtain the claim. \(\square\)

steps.title: Product-state and parameter convergence
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step, for every \(t\ge0\),

\[d_t\le\sqrt{\frac{2E(t)}\lambda},\qquad\sqrt{\frac{2E(t)}\lambda}\le\sqrt{\frac{2E(0)}\lambda}\,e^{-\lambda t},\qquad\|a_t-a_\star\|\le\sqrt{\frac{2E(0)}\lambda}\,e^{-\lambda t},\]

where \(E(t)=\mathcal E(t)-\mathcal E_\star\) and \(d_t=\sqrt{d_t^2}\).

Proof. By the previous step, \(E(t)\ge\frac\lambda2d_t^2\ge0\), and likewise \(E(0)\ge0\). Dividing the Talagrand bound by \(\lambda/2>0\) gives \(d_t^2\le2E(t)/\lambda\), and the square root is increasing on \([0,\infty)\). For the second inequality, the decay step with \(T=t\) gives \(E(t)\le E(0)e^{-2\lambda t}\); multiplying by \(2/\lambda>0\),

\[\frac{2E(t)}\lambda\le\frac{2E(0)}\lambda e^{-2\lambda t}=\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac{2E(0)}\lambda}\,e^{-\lambda t}\Bigr)^2,\]

and taking square roots of these nonnegative numbers gives the bound. Finally \(\|a_t-a_\star\|^2\le d_t^2\), because \(d_t^2\) is \(\|a_t-a_\star\|^2\) plus a nonnegative average of squared distances; combining with the first two inequalities gives the parameter bound. \(\square\)

Claim (Theorem 3.1, corrected). Let \(M\ge1\), \(\lambda>0\), and let \(U_1,\dots,U_M:\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_z}\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex (A3). Let \(\ell(a)=M^{-1}\sum_m\log\int e^{-U_m(a,z)}dz\). Then there is exactly one \(a_\star\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) such that

  1. \(\ell(a)\le\ell(a_\star)\) for every \(a\), and
  2. for every classical flow with comparison parameter \(a_\star\), constant \(\lambda\) and potentials \(U_m\), whose comparison densities are the posteriors \(q_\star^m=e^{-U_m(a_\star,\cdot)}/\int e^{-U_m(a_\star,w)}dw\), and for every \(t\ge0\), \[\|a_t-a_\star\|\le\sqrt{\frac{2(\mathcal E(0)-\mathcal E_\star)}\lambda}\,e^{-\lambda t}.\]

Proof. By the density-model section, \(\ell=-V\), where \(V\) is the average marginal potential. By the marginal section, \(V\) has exactly one minimizer \(a_\star\); hence \(a_\star\) is the unique maximizer of \(\ell\), which proves (1). For (2), A3 gives integrability of \(e^{-U_m(a,\cdot)}\) and positivity of its integral for all \(a\) (marginal section), so the hypotheses of the previous steps hold, and the parameter bound of the previous step is (2). Uniqueness: if \(b\) satisfies (1) and (2), then in particular \(\ell(a)\le\ell(b)\) for all \(a\), so \(V(b)\le V(a)\) for all \(a\), and \(b=a_\star\) by uniqueness of the minimizer of \(V\). \(\square\)

By the second step, \(\mathcal E_\star=-\ell(a_\star)=F_\star\) is the minimal free energy, so the prefactor is \(\sqrt{2(F(a_0,q_0)-F_\star)/\lambda}\) as in the paper. The theorem contains no assumed dissipation identity, log-Sobolev inequality or transport inequality; the only hypotheses beyond A3 are the extra assumptions defining a classical flow.

LatentDiffusion/Numerics.lean.title: Contractive Euler approximation and accumulated error
LatentDiffusion/Numerics.lean.summary: Work in a complete real inner-product space. The positive force \(F\) is \(m\)-strongly monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz: \(\langle F(x)-F(y),x-y\rangle\ge m\|x-y\|^2\) and \(\|F(x)-F(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\). Take \(m,h>0\), \(mh\le1\), and \(hL^2\le m\). The implemented force \(A\) can differ from \(F\). The numerical path is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-hA(x_k)+\xi_k\). A reference segment solves its actual integral equation with the same noise increment; its drift and noise sizes are explicit hypotheses, rather than an assumed numerical-error recurrence.

steps.title: Shared noise cancels in the contractive update
steps.body:
Claim. Under the force and step assumptions above, for any common increment \(\xi\), \(\|(x-hF(x)+\xi)-(y-hF(y)+\xi)\|\le q\|x-y\|\), where \(q=1-mh/2\in[0,1)\).

Proof. Put \(d=x-y\) and \(v=F(x)-F(y)\). The common increment cancels. Expanding the square and applying monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity gives

\[\|d-hv\|^2=\|d\|^2-2h\langle v,d\rangle+h^2\|v\|^2\le(1-2mh+h^2L^2)\|d\|^2\le(1-mh)\|d\|^2.\]

The last inequality uses \(hL^2\le m\), multiplied by \(h\ge0\). Since \(1-mh\le(1-mh/2)^2\) and \(q\ge0\), taking nonnegative square roots proves the claim. Positivity of \(mh\) gives \(q<1\). \(\square\)

steps.title: The local defect follows from the integral equation
steps.body:
Claim. Suppose every reference segment satisfies \(Y_k(0)=y_k\), \(Y_k(h)=y_{k+1}\), \(W_k(h)=\xi_k\), and

\[Y_k(t)-y_k=-\int_0^tF(Y_k(s))\,ds+W_k(t).\]

Assume the drift is interval integrable, \(\|F(Y_k(t))\|\le G\), and \(\|W_k(t)\|\le N\sqrt t\) for \(0\le t\le h\), with \(G,N\ge0\). Then the defect of a reference Euler step is at most \(R=L(h^2G/2+(2/3)h^{3/2}N)\).

Proof. The integral equation and the triangle inequality give \(\|Y_k(t)-y_k\|\le tG+N\sqrt t\). Subtract \(y_k-hF(y_k)+\xi_k\) from the endpoint equation; the noise increments cancel. The remaining vector is \(-\int_0^h(F(Y_k(s))-F(y_k))\,ds\). Its norm is at most

\[L\int_0^h\|Y_k(s)-y_k\|\,ds\le L\int_0^h(sG+N\sqrt s)\,ds=L\left(\frac{h^2G}{2}+\frac23h^{3/2}N\right).\]

The elementary integrals are \(h^2/2\) and \(2h^{3/2}/3\). In a random-state application the ambient norm is an \(L^2\) norm, so these same estimates are root-mean-square moment bounds. \(\square\)

steps.title: Iteration separates initial error, force bias and time discretisation
steps.body:
Claim. With the preceding hypotheses, suppose \(\|A(x_k)-F(x_k)\|\le B\) for every \(k\), where \(B\ge0\). Then

\[\|x_n-y_n\|\le q^n\|x_0-y_0\|+\frac{2B}{m}+\frac Lm\left(hG+\frac43N\sqrt h\right).\]

Proof. Insert two intermediate points, namely the Euler updates with force \(F\) at \(x_k\) and \(y_k\). The triangle inequality, the force error, the contraction and the local defect imply \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+hB+R\), where \(e_k=\|x_k-y_k\|\). Induction yields \(e_n\le q^ne_0+(hB+R)\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j\). Since \(0\le q<1\) and the forcing term is nonnegative, the finite sum is at most \(1/(1-q)=2/(mh)\). Hence

\[\frac{hB+R}{1-q}=\frac{2B}{m}+\frac Lm\left(hG+\frac43N\sqrt h\right).\]

The division is legitimate because \(m,h>0\). This proves the bound uniformly in the iteration count. It does not construct the reference path or establish its moment bounds for a new application. \(\square\)

Claim. The normalized force \(F\) is \(m\)-strongly monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz.

Summing the strong-convexity inequalities for the potentials therefore makes \(V\) \(Km\)-strongly convex. Differentiability follows by the chain rule and finite summation. For the gradient, the chain rule gives

\[\langle abla V(x)- abla V(y),w angle=\sum_i\langle abla U_i(J_ix)- abla U_i(J_iy),J_iw angle.\]

Lipschitz continuity, Cauchy-Schwarz for the finite sum, and the coordinate identity bound the absolute value by \(KL\|x-y\|\|w\|\). Taking the supremum over unit vectors gives \(\| abla V(x)- abla V(y)\|\le KL\|x-y\|\). Strong convexity similarly gives \(\langle abla V(x)- abla V(y),x-y angle\ge Km\|x-y\|^2\). Multiplication by \(1/K>0\) proves both assertions for \(F\). The argument allows distinct potentials and arbitrary finite parameter and latent dimensions. \(\square\)

steps.title: Independent score fluctuations yield the sampling term

Claim. Let \(Q\) be extraction of the parameter block, with operator norm at most one. Put \(V=\sum_i\mathbb E\|s_i-\mathbb Es_i\|^2\), \(G=\|F_{\rm frozen}(S_0)\|_{L^2}\), and let \(W\) denote the physical Brownian increment scale. The coupled full-batch trajectory satisfies

Stationarity preserves this residual norm at every reference time. The frozen integral equation supplies the reference segments used in the numerical comparison; its drift norm is \(G\), and Brownian increments supply the square-root-time scale \(W\). Apply the equilibrium-reference Euler comparison with this residual bound. The parameter block of \(S_t\) is constant. Finally \(\|Q(X_n-S_{nh})\|_{L^2}\le\|X_n-S_{nh}\|_{L^2}\) transfers the cloud estimate to the parameter estimate. \(\square\)

LatentDiffusion/RegularMeanField.lean.summary: Let the heterogeneous particle potentials be differentiable and jointly \(m\)-strongly convex, with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradients, and let the particle count be positive. Consider a continuous \(L^2(P)\) mean-field integral solution \(Y_t\) and a continuous stationary frozen-posterior solution \(S_t\) driven by the same physical Brownian path. Assume the posterior scores have zero total expectation, and the initial parameter of \(Y\) and the reference parameter of \(S\) are deterministic. The statement holds for any real \(m\); it gives decay when \(m>0\). Existence of a new solution is not asserted by a comparison of supplied solutions.

steps.title: Cancellation of common noise gives exponential parameter control
steps.body:
Claim. If the reference parameter is \(a_\star\), then for every \(t\ge0\), \(\|QY_t-a_\star\|_{L^2}\le e^{-mt}\|Y_0-S_0\|_{L^2}\).

Proof. Apply the parameter projection to the integral equation of \(Y\). The physical noise has zero parameter block, so its parameter remains the deterministic initial value minus the integral of the expected parameter force. The zero-score identity makes the frozen reference an admissible mean-field solution with constant parameter \(a_\star\). Subtract their two equations. Their common additive noise cancels. Strong monotonicity, including the deterministic-parameter expectation identities, gives the energy inequality \(\frac d{dt}\|Y_t-S_t\|_{L^2}^2\le-2m\|Y_t-S_t\|_{L^2}^2\). Multiply by \(e^{2mt}\); the derivative of the product is nonpositive. Integrating from zero to \(t\) gives \(\|Y_t-S_t\|_{L^2}^2\le e^{-2mt}\|Y_0-S_0\|_{L^2}^2\). Nonnegative square roots and the norm-one parameter projection finish the proof. Continuity and the supplied integral equations provide the time-integrability needed for this energy argument. \(\square\)

LatentDiffusion/RegularSourceTheorem.lea.title: A full-batch root-mean-square rate to the actual optimizer
LatentDiffusion/RegularSourceTheorem.lea.summary:
Let \(K=MN>0\). Assume \(m>0\), differentiable jointly \(m\)-strongly convex heterogeneous potentials with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradients, and a stable positive step. The optimizer \(a_\star\) is the actual marginal optimizer already constructed from these potentials.

Supply an \(L^2\) initial latent cloud with the stated frozen Gibbs law at \(a_\star\), the correct individual posterior marginals, the local domination assumptions for evidence differentiation, and independent initial posterior scores. The coordinate Brownian processes have independent scalar Euler increments, independent of the initial latent cloud. Suppose each centred score has second moment at most \(V_0\). These extra initialization, independence and differentiation assumptions are part of the theorem.

steps.title: Identify the optimizer, then insert explicit variance and Brownian constants
steps.body:
Claim. For the actual pointwise Euler recursion,

\[\left(\mathbb E\|a_n-a_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le q^nR_0+\frac2m\sqrt{\frac{V_0}{MN}}+\frac Lm\left(h\sqrt{L d_z}+\frac43\sqrt{2d_z}\sqrt h\right),\qquad q=1-mh/2,\]

where \(R_0\) is the \(L^2\) distance from the initial cloud to the scaled posterior cloud at \(a_\star\), and \(d_z\) is the dimension of one latent vector.

Proof. The evidence derivative at the optimizer centres the sum of posterior scores. The stipulated Gibbs initialization and independent Brownian increments furnish the stationary frozen reference used by the preceding stochastic comparison. Its frozen drift moment is bounded by \(\sqrt{Ld_z}\), and the scaled physical noise has increment norm \(\sqrt{2d_z}\sqrt t\). These facts give the three-term comparison with sampling residual \(K^{-1}\sqrt{\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(s_i)}\). The per-score bound gives \(\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(s_i)\le KV_0\), hence

\[\frac1K\sqrt{\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(s_i)}\le\frac{\sqrt{KV_0}}K=\sqrt{\frac{V_0}K}.\]

All factors are nonnegative and \(K>0\), so taking square roots and dividing preserves the inequality. Substitute \(K=MN\) and the explicit moment constants. The pointwise and lifted recursions agree in \(L^2\), which converts the projected norm to the displayed integral. No assertion of uniform complexity follows unless the constants stay bounded independently of particle count and step size. \(\square\)

LatentDiffusion/Accuracy.lean.title: Five explicit allocations of the requested error tolerance
LatentDiffusion/Accuracy.lean.summary: Let \(\varepsilon,m,K>0\), \(h,R_0,V,L,G,W\ge0\), and \(\sigma\in\mathbb R\). Suppose \(q=1-mh/2\ge0\) and an error \(E\) has the five-term upper bound \(q^nR_0+(2/m)\sqrt{V/K}+(L/m)hG+(4L/(3m))W\sqrt h+\sqrt{h\sigma^2/m}\). The following arithmetic allocates \(\varepsilon/5\) to each term. It applies after the stochastic/reference theorem supplies this upper bound; the arithmetic does not establish those hypotheses.

steps.title: Logarithmic burn-in and four algebraic restrictions
steps.body:
Claim. The error satisfies \(E\le\varepsilon\) if

\[\begin{gathered}\log\max\{1,5R_0/\varepsilon\}\le mhn/2,\qquad 100V\le m^2\varepsilon^2K,\\5LhG\le m\varepsilon,\qquad400L^2W^2h\le9m^2\varepsilon^2,\qquad25h\sigma^2\le m\varepsilon^2.\end{gathered}\]

Proof. The inequality \(1-u\le e^{-u}\), with \(u=mh/2\), and \(q\ge0\) imply \(q^nR_0\le e^{-mhn/2}R_0\). The logarithmic restriction makes this at most \(\varepsilon/5\); taking a maximum with one also covers \(R_0=0\) and an initial error already below tolerance. For the particle term, square its desired nonnegative inequality:

\[\left(\frac2m\sqrt{\frac VK}\right)^2\le\frac{\varepsilon^2}{25}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad100V\le m^2\varepsilon^2K.\]

The drift inequality is equivalent to its desired bound after multiplication by \(5m>0\). Squaring the nonnegative Brownian term gives exactly \(400L^2W^2h\le9m^2\varepsilon^2\). Squaring the oracle term gives exactly \(25h\sigma^2\le m\varepsilon^2\). Nonnegativity permits the square-root comparisons in each case. Thus the sum of all five terms is at most \(5\varepsilon/5=\varepsilon\). The division-free restrictions also make sense when variance, drift or noise constants vanish. \(\square\)
